title: Literacy as a Connected System
author: Richard Wheadon
summary: Wales' National Year of Reading risks replicating a familiar mistake: responding to a genuine priority by fragmenting literacy into another standalone initiative. Reviewing four Substack articles for a local authority newsletter, the author argues that vocabulary, morphology, reading, writing, and oracy form an integrated system in which each component strengthens the others. Research on expertise supports this: experts make better decisions not because they know more but because their knowledge is organized differently, into rich interconnected schemas. Professional learning that delivers isolated strategies — a vocabulary technique this term, a writing framework the next — is unlikely to develop the professional judgment that effective teaching requires. The challenge for Welsh education is not just to become better teachers of reading, but to develop the coherent mental models that allow teachers to understand when, why, and how any literacy strategy should be used.
points: Vocabulary, writing, reading, and oracy are not competing priorities but an integrated literacy system — each strengthens the others, and treating them as separate initiatives undermines all of them.

Research on expertise shows that experts do not make better decisions because they possess more knowledge but because that knowledge is organized differently, into interconnected schemas rather than isolated facts.

Dylan Wiliam argues that improving teaching is less about accumulating an ever-growing repertoire of techniques than developing the judgment to know which approach is appropriate in a particular context.

Haili Hughes' warning about the de-intellectualisation of teaching provides the conceptual thread: teachers are not delivery mechanisms for other people's ideas but professionals who draw on evidence to make complex judgements.
The real opportunity in Wales' Year of Reading is not simply to become better teachers of reading, but to develop coherent mental models of literacy that support informed professional judgment.
quotes: The greatest risk is not that we focus too much on reading, but that we respond by fragmenting literacy into another standalone initiative.
Reading, writing, vocabulary, and oracy are not separate priorities competing for schools’ attention. They form an integrated system in which each strengthens the others.
Experts recognise deep conceptual relationships where novices often notice only superficial features.
improving teaching is less about accumulating an ever-growing repertoire of techniques than developing the judgement to know which approach is appropriate in a particular context
None advocates another initiative. Instead, each challenges us to deepen our understanding of literacy itself.
If we support teachers to develop a richer understanding of how these elements connect, we strengthen their capacity to exercise informed professional judgement.
our challenge is not simply to become better teachers of reading. It is to become better teachers of literacy.
